annotationRationale: The method exhausts the bounded integer pairs for each relevant score and uses the prohibition on reusing cards to force Ravon's pair.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Prealgebra is appropriate for this bounded pair-sum deduction. No area repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: The forced deal is Oscar (1,3), Aditi (2,5), Ravon (4,7), Tyrone (6,10), and Kim (8,9). All scores agree, and C is the only true choice. No prompt, choice, grading, or figure contradiction is present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The supplied references use the same pair-elimination idea. LIVE's additional Tyrone case split is unnecessary once Ravon's pair is forced; no additional method is needed.
review.annotationCheck: The assessed integer-solutions node accurately captures exhaustive enumeration under finite integer bounds and elimination using unavailable cards. Empty support and context roles are appropriate.
review.areaCheck: Prealgebra is appropriate for this bounded pair-sum deduction. No area repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Oscar's only distinct-card pair summing to 4 is (1,3). Aditi's three listed possibilities exhaust the pairs summing to 7, leaving only (2,5). Ravon's five listed possibilities exhaust the pairs summing to 11; only (4,7) avoids the four assigned cards. Every decisive elimination is valid, so C follows independently.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: The Oscar-to-Aditi-to-Ravon sequence matches the supplied AoPS argument; LIVE supports the initial deductions before taking a longer Tyrone branch. Both references are correctly treated as third-party sources. The candidate supplies original explanatory prose and explicit pair enumeration, and source-informed-original is appropriate.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The opening explains why small scores are useful. The single-card restriction, complete pair lists, and elimination steps let an AMC 10 learner reconstruct the argument without additional prerequisites.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: math:integer-diophantine-equations directly fits the exhaustive bounded integer-pair reasoning used throughout. It is a central exact concept under the supplied definition.
